anf_compare.notes: An NPNF English exists under Basil, Letter 260; it was read only to confirm the text's identity and the two readings taken by sense, not for wording.

bible_refs.note: ζέων τῷ πνεύματι ('fervent in spirit') said of the addressee.

bible_refs.method: allusion: the sevenfold penalty of Cain from the LXX verse quoted in ep-open
bible_refs.note: The plain sense of the verse: Cain pays sevenfold.

choices.why: Aorist of διανίστημι, to rouse or raise up; the old men are woken, not arranged.
The writer speaks of his own age, numbed by time and bodily weakness.

choices.english: fervent in spirit (Romans 12:11), … us, who had grown cold
choices.why: ζέων is said of the addressee and quotes Romans 12:11; κατεψυγμένους is said of the writer.
rejected: you, who are living in spirit, are cooling us

choices.english: like animals that winter in their dens
choices.why: φωλεύω is to lie up in a den through the winter; a simile for waking from torpor.
rejected: from the state of animal lairs

choices.english: it can also admit a more varied explanation
choices.why: Read by sense as καὶ ποικίλον: the next sentence's 'the simpler sense' needs a second, more complex reading.
rejected: to receive a word that is unshakable

choices.term: δεῖ τὸν Καῒν ἑπταπλασίωνα δοῦναι τὴν τιμωρίαν
choices.english: Cain must pay a sevenfold penalty
choices.why: δοῦναι τὴν τιμωρίαν is to pay the penalty: Cain is the one who pays.
rejected: Cain must be given sevenfold the recompense

choices.english: if he himself is to be made better
choices.why: 'Or he will become better' makes no sense here; read as a condition.
rejected: or perhaps he himself will become better

choices.why: Οὐκοῦν opens the inference; the clause runs on into the next section.

lemmas.gloss: lie in a den, winter in a lair

pass_a_gloss: [continuing from 'first of all'] Then also us the old men, numbed already both by time and by the weakness of the body and by the great number of afflictions (for the many stirred up around us weighed down our life), you nevertheless roused up; and, boiling in the spirit, us who had been chilled, like the creatures among animals that lie up in dens, you lead back into a moderate wakefulness and a living activity. The saying, then, is able both to be understood simply in this way and [reading καὶ ποικίλον for ἀποίκιλον] to receive a varied account. The simpler meaning, then, the one able to come to everyone from what lies at hand, is this: that Cain must give the punishment sevenfold for the things in which he sinned. For it is not of a just judge to set equal repayments against equal [deeds]; but it is necessary for the one who started the evil to pay back what is owed with an addition, [reading ἢ μέλλει as a condition] if he himself is going to become better by the punishments and to make the others more self-controlled by the example. So then, since…
pass_b_english: Then, too, though we old men were already numbed by time, by the weakness of the body, and by the multitude of our afflictions (for the many that have stirred around us have weighed down our life), you have nevertheless roused us; and, fervent in spirit (Romans 12:11), you are bringing us, who had grown cold, back to a measure of wakefulness and lively activity, like animals that winter in their dens.
The saying, then, can be understood simply, as it stands, and it can also admit a more varied explanation.
The simpler sense, the one that can present itself readily to anyone, is this: that Cain must pay a sevenfold penalty for his sins (Genesis 4:15).

For it is not the part of a just judge to fix equal requitals for equal deeds; rather, the one who began the evil must repay what he owes with something added, if he himself is to be made better by the punishments and to make the rest more self-controlled by his example.
source_text:
Ἔπειτα καὶ ἡμᾶς τοὺς γέροντας νεναρκηκότας ἤδη καὶ τῷ χρόνῳ, καὶ τῇ
ἀσθενείᾳ τοῦ σώματος, καὶ τῷ πλήθει τῶν θλίψεων (αἱ πολλαὶ τοίνυν περὶ ἡμᾶς
κινηθεῖσαι ἐβάρησαν ἡμῶν τὴν ζωὴν), ὅμως διανέστησας, καὶ ζέων τῷ πνεύματι
κατεψυγμένους ἡμᾶς, ὡς τὰ φωλεύοντα τῶν ζώων εἰς ἐγρήγορσιν μετρίαν καὶ
ζωτικὴν ἐνέργειαν ἐπανάγεις. Ἔστιν οὖν τὸ ῥητὸν, καὶ ἀπλῶς οὕτω νοηθῆναι
δυνάμενον, καὶ ἀποίκιλον ἐπιδέξασθαι λόγον. Ἡ μὲν οὖν ἁπλουστέρα, καὶ παντὶ
δυναμένη ἐκ τοῦ προχείρου παραστῆσαι διάνοια, αὕτη ἐστίν· ὅτι δεῖ τὸν Καῒν
ἑπταπλασίωνα δοῦναι τὴν τιμωρίαν ὑπὲρ ὧν ἥμαρτεν. Οὐ γάρ ἐστι δικαιοκρίτου ἴσας
πρὸς ἴσας ὁρίζειν ἀνταποδόσεις· ἀλλ' ἀνάγκη τὸν κατάρξαντα κακοῦ μετὰ
προσθήκης ἀποτῖσαι τὰ ὀφειλόμενα, ἢ μέλλει αὐτὸς βελτίων ταῖς τιμωρίαις
γενέσθαι, καὶ τοὺς λοιποὺς σωφρονεστέρους ποιῆσαι τῷ ὑποδείγματι. Οὐκοῦν ἐπειδὴ
reviewer: claude (Wave A review, clause by clause against the Greek)
review_notes: Author: this letter is Basil of Caesarea's Letter 260, to Bishop Optimus. PG 77 prints it among the letters of Cyril of Alexandria as Letter 80.

Retranslated from the rv0 review: 'roused' for διανέστησας, 'old men' for γέροντας, 'fervent in spirit' (Romans 12:11), 'animals that winter in their dens', Cain as the one who pays, 'So then, since…' for Οὐκοῦν ἐπειδή; no opening ellipsis, since the sentence runs on from ep-open.
Copy-text readings taken by sense: ἀποίκιλον as καὶ ποικίλον; ἢ μέλλει as a condition.
